One static code holds one link

This is the part most app-store QR pages skip, so here it is plainly: a QR code stores text, and that text is a URL. One code, one destination. There is no logic inside the pattern that can look at the phone and pick a store.

That matters because your iOS and Android listings are two different URLs. A single static code can only point at one of them. If you encode the App Store link, Android users land on a page for an app they can't install, and the reverse is just as bad.
You have three ways to cover both platforms. The table below compares them.

Two codes is the honest, zero-effort option. Router page is what most apps do once they have a marketing site. Smart banners only work if people land on your site first, which is a different job from a printed code.
How to get your store links
Both stores give you a clean, permanent URL, and both are easy to find once you know where to look.

For iOS, open your app in App Store Connect, go to App Information, and copy the App Store URL. It looks like apps.apple.com/app/id1234567890. You can add a country segment — apps.apple.com/gb/app/id… — if you want the code to open a specific storefront, but the plain version redirects to the visitor's own region, which is usually what you want.

For Android, open the Play Console listing and copy the link from the browser bar. It looks like play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.yourcompany.yourapp. The id is your package name, and it never changes even when the app name does.

Drop anything after the ID. Marketing tools often append tracking parameters like ?mt=8 or &referrer=…. They're harmless, but they make the QR pattern denser for no benefit, and a denser pattern is harder to print small.
Building a router page that works
If you go with one code, it needs somewhere to send people. A router page is a small page on your own domain that reads the user agent and forwards.

The logic is short: if the browser reports an iPhone or iPad, go to the App Store; if it reports Android, go to Play; otherwise show both buttons. Keep a fallback for desktop, because a meaningful share of scans come from people testing on a laptop.

Two things break these pages in practice. Apple's in-app browsers and some social apps strip the user agent down to something generic, so the detection guesses wrong. And a redirect that fires before the page renders can look like a broken link. Showing both buttons with the detected one highlighted is more forgiving than an instant forward.
If you want the destination editable later, use a dynamic code pointing at the router page. Change the page and every printed code follows, no reprint.

When you print two codes, label them. A pair of identical-looking squares with no "iPhone" and "Android" text is worse than one code, because people scan the wrong one and land on a store they can't use.
Can one static code open both stores?

No. A static code stores a single URL, and your two store listings are two URLs. Encode the App Store link and Android visitors land on an app they cannot install. Print two labelled codes, or point one code at a page on your own domain that reads the phone and forwards to the right store.
What if I fill in both fields?
Only the App Store link is encoded — the Play field is used when the App Store field is empty. To cover both platforms, make two codes, one per field.
